title: COMP-MCCAA/08/2024 – Assessment of the Proposed full-function joint venture between Francis Busuttil & Sons (Marketing) Limited, JCP Holdings Limited and Pacikka Holdings Limited to establish NewCo, and acquire the assets held by the Good Earth group (Phase I Decision)
text:
Assessment of the Proposed full-function joint venture between Francis Busuttil & Sons
(Marketing) Limited, JCP Holdings Limited and Pacikka Holdings Limited to establish NewCo,
and acquire the assets held by the Good Earth group (Phase I Decision)
Office for Competition - Case COMP/MCCAA/08/2024
26 November 2024
Decision on Proposed Acquisition in terms of Regulations 6(1)(ii) of the Control of
Concentrations Regulations (LN 294 of 2002 as subsequently amended)
In accordance with Article 28 of the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority Act, any
information which the Office for Competition considered to be confidential and/or revealing business
secrets has been redacted from this version. All omissions are indicated by [✄]. Not all omissions
necessarily constitute confidential data.
Done at the Office for Competition, Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority, Mizzi House,
National Road, Blata l-Bajda, Malta on 26th November, 2024.

Members of the Office for Competition who conducted the Assessment of this concentration
Melchior Vella (Director, Primary Manufacturing and Retail Markets)
Sean Buttigieg (Senior Economics Manager)
Alexia Vella (Senior Professional Officer (Economics))
The Office for Competition would also like to thank Denise Camilleri (Director) for the valuable
contributions.
Office for Competition - 2 -

1 SUMMARY
1. On Friday, 11th October 2024, the Office for Competition (hereinafter referred to as “the
Office”) within the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority received notification of a
proposed concentration pursuant to Article 6 of the Control of Concentrations Regulations
(Subsidiary Legislation 379.08) between Francis Busuttil & Sons (Marketing) Limited (Santa
Venera), JCP Holdings Limited (Marsa) and Pacikka Holdings Limited (Naxxar).
2. The nature of the concentration is to establish a full-function joint venture (hereinafter referred
to as “JV”) between Francis Busuttil & Sons (Marketing) Limited, JCP Holdings Limited and
Pacikka Holdings Limited, to acquire the assets held by the Good Earth Group. The nature of
the JV’s business shall be the importation, manufacture, packaging, and distribution of fast-
moving consumer goods.
3. Francis Busuttil & Sons (Marketing) Limited forms part of the group of companies of Francis
Busuttil & Sons Limited (hereinafter referred to as “FBS group”) which is involved in the
business of manufacture and distribution of food and beverage and importation and distribution
of fast-moving consumer goods through its various subsidiaries. JCP Holdings Limited
manufactures, imports and distributes through its group of companies a wide range of frozen
and chilled products in retail and hotel, restaurant and catering establishments. Pacikka
Holdings Limited is the holding company of Joinwell Limited which is involved in the
manufacture and retail of furniture. The Good Earth Group is an importer, wholesaler, exporter
and retailer of different raw materials and finished food products, including partly processed
and processed materials relating to foodstuffs and beverages. It also carries out the business
of manufacturing and processing of various foodstuffs and beverages.
4. After a detailed competitive assessment of the proposed concentration, the Office concludes
that the concentration will not lead to a substantial lessening of competition (hereinafter referred
to as “SLC”) in the affected markets, since the involved parties will continue to face strong
competition.
2 THE PARTIES
5. Francis Busuttil & Sons (Marketing) Limited, (hereinafter referred to as “FBSM”) having
company registration number C 24137, is a private limited liability company organised and
existing under the laws of Malta. Its registered office is at Busuttil Buildings, Santa Venera
Square, Santa Venera, SVR1681, Malta. In 2023, FBS group generated a turnover of [✄] in
Malta, out of which [✄] was generated by FBSM.
6. JCP Holdings Limited, (hereinafter referred to as “JCP”) having company registration number
C 99982, is a private limited company organised and existing under the laws of Malta. Its
registered office is at 1, Pastoral House, Second Floor, Prince Albert Street, Albert Town,
Marsa, MRS1041, Malta. For the financial period, 16 August 2021 to 31 December 2022, the
company generated a total turnover of [✄] in Malta.
7. Pacikka Holdings Limited, (hereinafter referred to as “Pacikka”), having company registration
number C 108470, has only been recently incorporated and it wholly owns Joinwell Limited. Its
registered office is at Warehouse No 1, Hard Rocks Industrial Park, Triq Burmarrad, Naxxar,
NXR 6345, Malta. Pacikka currently holds Joinwell Limited having company registration number
C 27929, which as at 2022, generated a turnover of [✄] in Malta. Pacikka is jointly controlled
by Nikolai de Giorgio and Sebastion de Giorgio. Furthermore, Nikolai de Giorgio has joint
Office for Competition - 3 -

control with a third party in Horizon Group Limited which holds Exco Services Limited, where
the turnover in Malta generated in 2023 by Exco, attributed to Nikolai de Giorgio stood
approximately at [✄].
8. FBSM, JCP and Pacikka shall together be referred to as “the Notifying Parties”.
9. Good Earth Distributors Limited, (hereinafter referred to as “GEDL”), having company
registration number C 6370 is a private limited company and the parent company of Good Earth
Importers Limited (having company registration number C 62705). Their registered office is at
Hard Rocks Industrial Estate, Wied il-Għasel, Burmarrad, Naxxar, NXR 6345, Malta and
together they constitute the Good Earth Group (hereinafter referred to as “GE Group”). For the
year 2022, GEDL generated approx. [✄] in turnover.
10. Only the business and assets of the GE Group (hereinafter referred to as “The Target
Business” or “the Target”) are subject to the Transaction.
11. The Notifying Parties and the Target shall together be referred to as “the Parties”.
3 PROPOSED TRANSACTION
12. Pursuant to a Memorandum of Understanding (hereinafter referred to as “MOU”) signed on
30th September 2024, the proposed transaction involves the establishment of a full-function JV
(hereinafter referred to as “NewCo”) between FBSM, JCP and Pacikka, to acquire the assets
held by the GE Group and it will be jointly controlled by the Notifying Parties. The nature of the
JV’s business shall be the importation, manufacture, packaging and the distribution of fast-
moving consumer goods (hereinafter “the Proposed Transaction” or “the Transaction”).
13. [✄]. The JV shall be jointly controlled by all three Notifying Parties. [✄].
14. The Proposed Transaction [✄]. The efficiencies to be derived from the Transaction should thus
be substantial and timely, benefitting consumers. The efficiencies are merger-specific, in that
the new investment injected in the Target Business would not be possible without the
concentration. The efficiencies are also likely to be realised, in that the Notifying Parties, having
invested in NewCo, all have an interest in securing the immediate success and growth of the
JV on the market.
15. The Proposed Transaction is conditional on the clearance by the Office for Competition,
declaring the transaction a lawful concentration in terms of the Control of Concentration
Regulations. The proposed concentration is not subject to review by any other competition
authority.
4 LEGAL BASIS AND JURISDICTION
16. According to Regulation 4 of the Control of Concentrations Regulations, it shall be the duty of
the Director General of the Office for Competition to determine whether a concentration leads
to an SLC in the Maltese market or a part thereof and if so, prohibit it.
17. The Office considers that the JV will perform on a lasting basis all the functions of an
autonomous economic entity within the meaning of Regulation 2 of the Control of
Concentrations Regulations and that the proposed transaction thus constitutes a concentration.
Office for Competition - 4 -

18. Furthermore, regulation 6(1) (ii) of the Control of Concentrations Regulations holds that where
the Director General of the Office for Competition finds that the concentration notified, although
falling within the scope of these Regulations, does not raise serious doubts about its lawfulness
in terms of the provisions of these Regulations, the Director General of the Office for
Competition shall decide not to oppose it and shall declare it to be a lawful concentration and
such a declaration shall also cover restrictions directly related and necessary to the
implementation of the concentration.
5 PROCEDURE
19. The Office conducted meetings with the authorised representative of the Notifying Parties and
also had a number of exchanges prior to the notification of concentration. The notification of
concentration was deemed complete on 11th October 2024.
20. The filing and acceptance of the concentration notification was notified to the public through a
notice that appeared in a local daily newspaper, on the Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs
Authority's website1 and a public notice that appeared in the Government Gazette (No. 26,995)2
on Tuesday, 22 October 2024.
21. In compiling the competitive assessment, the Office has relied on relevant guidelines issued by
the European Commission and on European competition case law.
22. In its assessment, the Office has also relied on three main sources of data (i) information
submitted by the Notifying Parties (ii) Requests for Information (hereinafter referred to as “RFI”)
sent to the Parties, (iii) RFI sent to the competitors operating in the same market as the involved
Parties, more specifically in the plant-based milk and other plant-based products, such as
desserts. Among other things, the scope of the RFI, was for the Office to define and assess the
size of the product market and ask for views on the proposed acquisition.
5.1 Third-Party Views
23. The Office received a number of third-party concerns from other players present in either the
wholesale or retail markets or both for plant-based milk and other plant-based products, such
as desserts. The concerns are summarised below:
a. This concentration could result in a monopoly and could create unfair competition and
impose conditions to retailers/consumers.
b. This concentration could result in less favourable terms for retailers, including shorter
credit periods, limited refunds on expired products, and potentially lower profit margins,
affecting retailer profitability.
c. There is a fear that potential monopolistic behaviour could lead to unfair competition,
harming smaller businesses unable to compete with large, consolidated firms.
d. Fear that smaller businesses are being pushed out by larger companies where the
focus is on price and volume over quality and sustainability. This dynamic may
1 Notification of Concentration < https://www.mccaa.org.mt/Section/Content?contentId=11352 > last accessed on 30 October
2024
2Notification of Concentration <
https://govcms.gov.mt/en/Government/DOI/Government%20Gazette/Documents/2024/10/Government%20Gazette%20-

Office for Competition - 5 -

ultimately harm consumers, who are wiped out by aggressive marketing toward lower-
quality, brand-driven products.
24. In their reply to the third-party comments, the Notifying Parties explained that the proposed JV
will operate autonomously and independently from its parent companies, and that FBSM and
JCP will continue with their current operations and business activities separately from NewCo
and from each other as they presently do. The Parties have not identified any market where
post-transaction a monopoly would result. In all the markets, where an overlap has been
identified ample scope for competition remains, namely because of the existence of several
other competing brands and private label products (hence competitors) on the market, the
existence of parallel trade, low barriers to entry and expansion, and the possibility of potential
competition as several other competing brands not yet present on the market in Malta already
exist in the EU and the wider market. Furthermore, the Parties have not identified any market
where no overlap exists and where individually they hold a market share above 25%. The
Parties highlighted that due to significant existing and potential parallel trade and aggressive
competition the Transaction could not create a monopoly in any relevant product market, let
alone in the food distribution or retail sector market in general. Nor could it lead to the imposition
of unfair conditions on retailers and consumers.
25. On the second point, the Notifying Parties contended that the Proposed Transaction is not
going to increase the market power of the JV or the Notifying Parties, as they will remain
disciplined by actual and potential competition constraints. Consequently, the Transaction
should not per se impact the commercial terms offered by the JV or the Notifying Parties.
Commercial terms will continue to be established independently by the Notifying Parties and
the JV in line with their individual commercial policies. Thus, for instance, credit terms would
be determined according to each Party’s objective criteria, such as their individual appreciation
of the risk involved.
26. On the second point, the Notifying Parties also clarify that the concern raised is unfounded for
the following reasons:
a. In this sector, retailers, particularly larger ones such as supermarkets, generally hold
the (buyer) power. This dynamic frequently results in conditions being imposed on
distributors rather than the other way round. For example, while consumers are
generally unable to return expired products to retailers, distributors may still be required
to accept returns of expired products from retailers, even if these were initially sold in
good condition and within valid expiration dates. This practice is often driven by the
substantial pressure that larger retailers exert over distributors.
b. [✄].
27. On the third observation, the Notifying Parties explained that the proposed concentration does
not lead to a monopoly, and neither will it give the JV or the Notifying Parties market power.
Hence, any such fear is unwarranted in the circumstances. This apart, and as an aside from
the Proposed Transaction, it should be observed that consolidation in certain circumstances is
capable of producing beneficial effects for customers, particularly smaller retailers. In a world
where national distributors increasingly face pressure from retailers seeking higher profit
margins, and the brand owners they represent to respect standards, consolidation enables
distributors to reduce their cost base, allowing them to remain viable and offer competitive
pricing and conditions to compete with international retail players and local retail chains
promoting private label products. Further, certain costs, such as warehousing and distribution
costs, have risen sharply due to soaring property prices, traffic issues, and labour shortages,
threatening the viability of national distributors. Yet, the viability and continued existence of
distributors is, in fact, crucial for the smaller retailers which due to the absence of economies
Office for Competition - 6 -

of scale are themselves unable to engage in imports and, consequently, rely on distributors’
continued presence to source goods. Hence, as international retailers and private label brands
continue to gain significant strength on the Maltese market, the distributors’ continued existence
is imperative not only to exert competitive pressure on international retailers and larger
supermarkets, but also to ensure that smaller retailers are not wiped out of the market due to
the absence of independent distributors able to supply them, leaving the market to be
dominated by the international players and larger supermarkets.
28. Lastly, on the last observation made by the third parties, the Parties commented that the
concentration will not confer market power upon the JV or the Notifying Parties. This apart, the
Parties to the Transaction adhere to high compliance standards, meeting brand owner quality
requirements and local regulatory standards and obligations, such as, maintaining refrigerated
transport and warehouses, among other requirements.
6 RELEVANT MARKET
29. This section defines the appropriate definition of the product market for the purpose of providing
the framework for the competitive assessment of the proposed concentration.
30. The relevant product market concept implies that there can be effective competition between
the products that form part of it. In the European Commission’s notice on market definition, it is
stated that “The relevant product market comprises all those products that customers regard
as interchangeable or substitutable to the product(s) of the undertaking(s) involved, based on
the products’ characteristics, their prices and their intended use, taking into consideration the
conditions of competition and the structure of supply and demand on the market”.3
31. When defining the relevant product market, the Office has taken into account factors related to
both demand and supply.
32. The Parties are all food distributors in Malta and thus, they overlap on some markets. Thus, the
notified transaction will create a horizontal overlap between the Notifying Parties and the
Target.
6.1 Product Scope
33. The relevant market concept implies that there can be effective competition between the
products that form part of it. In the European Commission’s notice on market definition, it is
stated that “a relevant product market comprises all those products and/or services which are
regarded as interchangeable or substitutable by the consumer, by reason of the products’
characteristics, their prices and their intended use”. 4
34. The Office considers that there are three relevant product markets.5 The relevant markets
examined are:
a. Plant-based milk
3 Commission Notice on the definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Union competition law (C/2024/1645), para 12.
4 Commission Notice on the definition of the relevant market for the purposes of Union competition law (C/2024/1645), para 6.
5 Overlap between the parties to the concentration exists in product markets such as herbs & spices, biscuits, and crackers.
However, since the combined market share post-concentration will remain below 15%, these markets do not meet the threshold
for being considered affected markets, as defined by instances where two or more parties to the concentration are engaged in
the same product market and the concentration results in a combined market share of 15% or more.
Office for Competition - 7 -

b. Tea
c. Cereal
35. The above are the markets in which the Parties significantly overlap. Other markets where the
overlap is insignificant, were not considered.6 This is also in line with the submissions made to
the Office by the Notifying Parties.
6.1.1 Plant-Based Milk
36. The Target and one of the Notifying Parties, FBSM, both distribute different brands of plant-
based milk and other plant-based products, such as desserts, in Malta. The Target supplies the
Alpro brand, whilst FBSM supplies the Valsoia and the Riso Scotti brands.
6.1.1.1 Consumer trends
37. Plant-based products are derived from different sources, which can be classified according to
raw materials. Plant‐based beverages can be generally classified in four categories: cereal‐
based (e.g., oat, rice); legumes‐based (e.g., soy, peanut, lupin, cowpea); nut‐based (e.g.,
almond, coconut, hazelnut, sunflower); and pseudocereals‐based (e.g., quinoa, teff,
amaranth).7 This classification reflects the broad spectrum of products that consumers can
choose from, enhancing the market's appeal. Furthermore, the introduction of innovative
flavours and formulations, such as those enhanced with probiotics or fortified with vitamins, has
contributed to the diversification of plant-based milk brands.
38. International research reports that the consumption of plant-based milk alternatives has seen
a significant increase in recent years, driven by various factors including health consciousness,
environmental concerns, and changing consumer preferences. Recent international research
indicates a notable shift in consumer behaviour towards plant-based milk alternatives, with
sales of these products more than doubling at the cost of traditional cow’s milk consumption.8
This trend is attributed to a combination of factors, including the perception of plant-based milk
as healthier and more sustainable options compared to dairy milk.9 The growing awareness of
lactose intolerance and dietary restrictions has also contributed to the rising popularity of plant-
based alternatives, as they cater to individuals who cannot consume dairy.10 Furthermore,
studies have shown that consumers are increasingly motivated by ethical considerations

Office for Competition - 8 -

regarding animal welfare and environmental sustainability, which further drives the demand for
plant-based options.11
39. Plant-based milk alternatives, while resembling animal milk in appearance and texture, vary
considerably in nutritional value and bioavailability. Therefore, fortifying these products is
essential to improve their nutritional profile.12 Additionally, while some consumers may switch
to plant-based milk for health reasons, others may remain loyal to dairy due to taste preferences
and the sensory experience associated with traditional milk.13
40. Recent research indicates that taste is a primary driver of consumer preference when it comes
to milk alternatives. Slade (2024) notes that there are substantial differences in taste
perceptions between consumers of plant-based milk alternatives and those who primarily
consume dairy milk.14 This finding is echoed by Cardello et al. (2022), who emphasise that
flavour profiles significantly influence consumer acceptance of plant-based products. The study
highlights that while some consumers appreciate the unique flavours of plant-based milk, others
may find them less appealing compared to the familiar taste of dairy milk.15 This discrepancy in
taste perception can lead to a reluctance among traditional dairy consumers to switch to plant-
based alternatives.
41. The economic dynamics between plant-based and dairy milk also reveal complexities in their
substitutability. Research has shown that while increasing sales of plant-based milk correlate
with a decline in dairy milk sales, the two are not perfect substitutes.16 A growing body of
research also examines the relationships between plant-based milk and dairy milk by
estimating cross-price elasticity, which measures how the quantity demanded of one product
changes in response to the price change of another. Dhar and Foltz (2005) found that early
commercial soymilk products were substitutes only for flavoured dairy milk.17 Using more recent
data, Dharmasena and Capps (2014) showed that soy milk serves as a substitute for plain dairy
milk across all types.18 Copeland and Dharmasena (2017) found a similar substitution pattern
between soy and dairy milk but noted a complementary relationship between almond and dairy
milk.19 Slade (2024) found that most consumers of milk alternatives also drink dairy milk, with
preferences varying by consumption context. A mixed logit model was used to estimate
consumer preferences of Canadians, which were then applied to calculate price elasticities and
predict market shares for dairy milk in scenarios excluding some milk alternatives. Despite a

low-price elasticity, the study predicted that 57% to 83% of milk alternative consumers would
have switched to dairy milk if alternatives were unavailable. Preferences for milk alternatives
were also influenced by age and food values, though treatment effects on the impacts of dairy
milk on animal welfare, the environment, and nutrition had generally insignificant effects.20
42. Factors such as price stability and consumer preferences for taste and texture play significant
roles in this relationship. For example, while some consumers are willing to try plant-based
alternatives, their overall preference for the taste of dairy milk can hinder a complete
transition.21 Additionally, the sensory attributes of plant-based milk, including sweetness and
flavour, significantly influence consumer acceptance and willingness to substitute.22
43. The European plant-based milk market has witnessed a remarkable increase in the number of
brands and product offerings. Major players such as Alpro, Innocent, Oatly, and Sojade have
established themselves as important brands in the sector, offering a range of products including
almond, oat, soy, and coconut milk alternatives. Alpro, a subsidiary of Danone, is particularly
noteworthy for its extensive portfolio of plant-based products, which includes not only milk
alternatives but also yogurt and desserts. Oatly, known for its oat milk, has gained significant
traction due to its marketing strategy that emphasises sustainability and health benefits. Other
notable brands include Califia Farms, Rude Health, and Minor Figures, each contributing to the
diverse landscape of plant-based milk options available to consumers. Other notable players
in the plant-based sector include Sojasun, Vive Soy, Valsoia, Natrue, Blue Diamond, and
Essential Waitrose Oat.
44. From the consumer perspective, private label brands offer a competitive alternative to
manufacturer brands, primarily because of their lower prices, which stem from reduced
production costs.23 Initially, these brands were mainly associated with price-sensitive shoppers.
However, today, consumers across various demographics are choosing private labels, as they
seek quality products at more affordable prices.24 From the retailer’s viewpoint, private label
brands play an important role in shaping their competitive strategy and differentiation. They can
enhance the store’s reputation, boost the retailer’s brand image, and foster customer loyalty.25
45. The substitutability between private-label and branded plant-based milk is influenced by several
factors, including price sensitivity, quality perception, and consumer demographics. Lindström
(2022) notes that demand for branded plant-based milk tends to be less elastic compared to
private-label products, indicating that consumers may be less sensitive to price changes for
branded options.26 This suggests that branded products can maintain higher price points due
to perceived quality and brand loyalty. Conversely, private-label products often compete on
price, appealing to budget-conscious consumers who prioritise cost over brand reputation. Li
et al. (2018) found that private-label milk products have higher markups despite being priced
lower than branded alternatives.27 This phenomenon can be attributed to lower marginal costs

associated with private-label production, allowing retailers to maintain profitability while offering
competitive prices. Furthermore, Kotler and Keller (2019) indicate that retailers are increasingly
developing exclusive store brands and are also adding premium private label brand items (also
called value-added private labels) to their private label brand assortments to differentiate
themselves from competitors.28 Vale et al. (2016) concluded that the main factor for consumers’
private label loyalty is the perceived quality.29 While the initial positioning strategy of private
label brands was based on low price, their study shows evidence that the adoption of private

6.1.1.2 Past cases
46. In past cases, the European Commission describes that plant-based products are derived from
plants rather than animal milk. They are primarily made from soy, but can also be made from
almonds, coconut, hazelnuts, or other types of plants and cereals. Similar to dairy products,
plant-based options include items like milk, yogurt, desserts, and cream. Originally, the plant-
based milk was created for those who were intolerant to dairy products but the mitigation of
plant base on taste and consumers’ change in eating habits, have created an increased
demand for plant-based products. Furthermore, it was regarded that while the dairy market is
on declining trend, the plant-based market is experiencing a growing trend.30 In a recent
German case they refer to plant-based products as an alternative to dairy products.31
47. In line with the above, the Parties submitted that these trends can also be applied to the Maltese
market since the plant-based industry is winning customers from the dairy market, indicating
an element of substitutability between the two.
48. With regards to product categories in the dairy sector, the Commission has segmented for
instance dairy milk from cream or desserts. However when comparing dairy-based desserts to
plant-based ones in M.8150, the Commission noted that plant-based and dairy-based desserts
cannot necessarily be regarded as separate product markets.32 It was also found that branded
and private label yoghurts compete with each other both in the dairy and plant-based
segments.33 The Commission also considers that the difference in plant within the plant-based
segment is not relevant, as customers tend to perceive the plant-based category as one.34
49. In past cases, the Commission adopted mixed views on the exact market definition of milk.
Albeit leaving the market definition open, the Commission appeared prepared to differentiate
between dairy-based milk and plant-based milk.35 In other cases, the Commission concluded
that plant-based and dairy-based yoghurts and desserts cannot necessarily be regarded as
separate product markets.36

6.1.1.3 Insights from undertakings on the product market
54. On the 23rd of October 2024, in order to assess the size of the product market and gather the
views of the competitors operating in the plant-based milk and other plant-based products, such
as desserts, the Office issued an RFI to undertakings involved in importation of plant-based
products.
55. From the data collected, 38% of importers of plant-based products in Malta believe that plant-
based milk moderately competes with dairy milk for the same consumer demand. Additionally,
12.5% indicated that plant-based and dairy products compete considerably, while another
12.5% stated that they compete very strongly. On the other hand, 63% of respondents reported
that the presence of dairy milk does not significantly affect the sales of plant-based alternatives.
56. Regarding consumer behaviour, many importers (69%) observed that customers who purchase
plant-based milk, yogurt, or desserts tend to switch between dairy and plant-based products.
The largest group (38%) observed a small portion of customers switching, with an increasing
trend. 19% noted a substantial portion switching, with a significant increase over time. 25%
reported no evidence of this behaviour, whereas smaller percentages observed stable trends
or were unsure. Some respondents attributed this growth to factors such as the rise in

veganism, a higher prevalence of lactose intolerance, a demand for greater variety, and
younger generations favouring healthier lifestyles.
57. Furthermore, 81% of suppliers reported observing either growth in plant-based consumption or
increased competition between dairy and plant-based products. Most highlighted significant
growth in plant-based consumption among Maltese consumers. Despite this trend, suppliers
anticipate that while plant-based demand will continue to grow, the demand for dairy products
will remain relatively strong.
58. When asked whether plant-based and dairy products can be considered substitutes, opinions
were divided. While 56% suggested that plant-based and dairy products are substitutable at
first glance, only 6% believed they fulfil the same needs or cater to the same consumer
segments. In contrast, 44% argued that plant-based and dairy products are not substitutable,
serving distinct needs and targeting different consumer segments.
59. Additionally, 81% of importers agreed that private-label plant-based products compete with
branded options, primarily on price. However, 31% of these importers think that branded
products continue to dominate the Maltese market. 19% of importers contend that that private-

60. Regarding the importance of plant-based milk imported by the Target Business in the hospitality
sector, 38% noted that Alpro is particularly demanded by cafés and restaurants due to its strong
brand reputation and extensive product range. Meanwhile, 31% argued that other plant-based

61. The majority of importers believe that plant-based milk competes with dairy milk for consumer
demand, with little impact on dairy milk sales. While consumer switching between the two is
increasing, the exact extent is unclear. Plant-based consumption has risen, although dairy
demand remains steady. Opinions on substitutability are mixed: some see them as
interchangeable, but only a small portion believe they fulfil the same needs. The rest view them
as distinct products for different consumer segments. Private-label plant-based products
compete well with branded options, though branded products still dominate in Malta. In the
OOH sector, Alpro is noted for its strong demand due to its reputation and variety, with other
brands also being popular.
6.1.1.4 Conclusion
62. In conclusion, the Parties put forward in their submission that both the dairy and plant-based
milk are part of the same market and that the market should be defined as branded and private
label dairy and plant-based milk for the retail sectors.
63. The Office considers that the literature shows a growing shift towards consuming plant-based
milk alternatives. However, the extent to which these products can replace traditional dairy milk
is complex, as differences in nutritional content and varying consumer preferences influence
their substitutability. Indeed, this mixed view on the degree of substitutability has been
confirmed by the questionnaire sent to a number of importers. It is also important to consider
that for vegans and individuals with lactose intolerance, the degree of substitutability is
effectively zero, due to their dietary restrictions, leaving them with no option but to consume
plant-based milk.
64. For the purpose of this decision, the exact product market definition, i.e. whether dairy-based
milk and plant-based milk/desserts form part of the same market, is left open as it will not affect
the outcome of the competitive assessment of this Proposed Transaction.

7.1 Horizontal non-coordinated effects
7.1.1 Analytical framework
85. The Commission Guidelines on the assessment of horizontal mergers under the Council
Regulation on the control of concentrations between undertakings (the “Horizontal Merger
Guidelines”)41 distinguish between two main ways in which mergers between actual or
potential competitors on the same relevant market may significantly impede effective
competition, namely non-coordinated and coordinated effects.
86. In each relevant market identified, the Parties argue that JV and only one of its parent
companies, either FBSM or JCP, will maintain activities in the same market as the JV. Pacikka
does not engage in economic activities in the markets where the JV will operate, and FBSM
and JCP are not aware of any product market where both would be active alongside the JV.
Therefore, no coordination effects are expected to arise between FBSM and JCP. The
Transaction is not expected to create cooperative effects among the parent companies. FBSM
and JCP will continue their normal operations independently in all markets where they are
already active, including the identified markets, and will carry out their economic activities
41 OJ C 31, 5.2.2004, p. 5.
Office for Competition - 16 -

independently of each other and of NewCo. [✄]. For these reasons, the Office considered that
the Transaction did not require a detailed assessment of coordinated effects.
87. Non-coordinated effects may significantly impede effective competition by eliminating important
competitive constraints on one or more firms, which consequently would have increased market
power, without resorting to coordinated behaviour. In that regard, the Horizontal Merger
Guidelines consider not only the direct loss of competition between the merging firms, but also
the reduction in competitive pressure on non-merging firms in the same market that could be
brought about by the merger.42
88. The Horizontal Merger Guidelines list a number of factors, which may influence the rise of
substantial non-coordinated, effects from a merger, such as: the large market shares of the
merging firms; the fact that the merging firms are close competitors; the limited possibilities for
customers to switch suppliers; or the fact that the merger would eliminate an important
competitive force. That list of factors applies equally if a merger would create or strengthen a
dominant position, or would otherwise significantly impede effective competition due to non-
coordinated effects. Furthermore, not all factors need to be present to make significant non-
coordinated effects likely and this is not an exhaustive list.43
89. Moreover, in assessing whether a concentration leads to a substantial lessening of competition,
the Office will also consider the third-party views.

7.1.3 Tea
110. As indicated in paragraph 68 of this Decision, the Office has left open the exact market definition
of the tea products, and will not be distinguishing between black, green and fruit/herbal infusion
teas, as even though the combined market share of the Notifying Parties and the Target
Business exceeds the 15% threshold as stipulated in the Control of Concentration Regulation,
the Office opines that there are no competition concerns in the tea market.
111. The Notifying Parties provided data for black and green tea based on the NSO statistics of
specific HS Codes, namely HS Codes 09023000 and 09024000 for black tea, and HS Codes
09021000 and 09022000 for green tea, while data for the fruit/herbal infusion tea was provided
through an estimate based on experience and knowledge of the market by the Notifying Parties.
The Office conducted a verification exercise and confirms that the data provided is accurate.
112. The market shares for these tea products, including those of FBSM and the Target Business,
were calculated for the period 2021-2023 based on total retail sales value. The Office observes
that the Target Business holds a minimal market share across all tea categories and that it
concurs with the Notifying Parties that the transaction will not strengthen FBSM's position in
the tea market, as amongst others, it does not eliminate a significant competitive constraint.
113. The Office notes that even though the market shares of FBSM tea products are high, they have
been on a downward trend from 2021 to 2023, indicating that FBSM is facing competitive
constraints on the tea market. Moreover, the Office notes that the combined market share of
FBSM and the Target Business remains below [✄], meaning that the greater part of the market
remains contestable by competitors.
114. The Office notes, as was the case for its assessment of the plant-based milk market, that there
a number of competing brands and private-label brands in the tea market, which seek to further
open the market for competition. The fact that there are also no barriers to entry and expansion
for new tea brands to be imported into the Maltese market, and the fact that there exist many
more brands available on the European market, serve to sustain the argument that the tea
market is quite dynamic, and that the Office concurs with the Notifying Parties’ competitive
assessment.
115. In view of the above, the Office concludes that the concentration will not lead to a substantial
lessening of competition and the involved parties will continue to face strong competition in the
relevant tea market concerned.
7.1.4 Cereal
116. The Office has left open the exact market definition of the cereal market, as was indicated in
paragraph 75 of this Decision. The Office opines that even though the combined market share
of the Notifying Parties and the Target Business in the cereal market exceeds the 15%

117. The Notifying Parties provided data for cereal products based on the NSO statistics of specific

19042095, 19042099 and 19049080. The market shares for cereal products, for both FBSM

based on the total value of sales in the retail sector. The Office conducted a verification exercise
and confirmed that the data provided is accurate. The Office notes, from the competitive
assessment made in the CN Form, that the combined market shares in the cereal market for
FBSM and the Target Business has decreased from [✄]% in 2021 to [✄]% in 2023.
118. The Office also observes that the market share of the Target Business for its cereal products
is quite marginal, and thus concurs with the Notifying Parties that this will not serve to
strengthen FBSM’s position, nor will it remove an important competitive constraint from the
market.
119. The Office considers that even though the market shares of FBSM cereal products are slightly
high, they have been on a downwards trend from 2021 to 2023, indicating that FBSM is facing
competitive constraints on the cereal market. Moreover, the Office notes that the combined
market share of FBSM and the Target Business remains below [✄], meaning that the greater
part of the market remains contestable by competitors.
120. The Office notes, as was the case for its assessment of the plant-based milk market and the
tea market, that there are a number of competing brands and private-label brands in the cereal
market, which seek to further open the market for competition. The Office concurs with the
Notifying Parties that there are also no barriers to entry and expansion for new cereal brands
to be imported into the Maltese market, and the fact that there exist many more brands available
on the European market, serve to sustain the Office’s argument that the cereal market is quite
dynamic, and that the Office concurs with the Notifying Parties’ overall competitive assessment.
121. In view of the above, the Office concludes that the concentration will not lead to a substantial
lessening of competition and the involved parties will continue to face strong competition in the
relevant cereal market concerned.

8 DECISION
122. In light of the above considerations, and in terms of Regulation 6(1)(ii) of the Control of
Concentrations Regulations, it is therefore decided:
a. That the Concentration falls within the scope of the Regulations on Control of
Concentrations;
b. That the Concentration does not raise serious doubts as to its lawfulness; and
c. Not to oppose the notified Concentration and to declare it a lawful Concentration.
